lessons.title: Performance Metrics Beyond Sharpe: Sortino, Calmar, and Tail Risk

body.text: Sharpe ratio treats a good surprise and a bad surprise as equally troubling, and says nothing at all about how bad the bad days can get. This lesson builds the rest of the report card a trained agent actually needs before anyone trusts it.

children.text: Chapter 3's reward design lesson already flagged Sharpe ratio's main limitation: it penalizes volatility symmetrically, an unusually good week hurts a Sharpe ratio almost as much as an unusually bad one, since both raise the standard deviation in the denominator. No trader actually wants to penalize a good surprise. This lesson builds three complements that address different blind spots Sharpe alone leaves open.
Sortino Ratio: Only Penalizing Downside Volatility

body.caption: The Sortino ratio uses the same numerator as Sharpe, excess return over a minimum acceptable return (MAR, often zero), but divides only by downside deviation: the volatility of returns that fell short of the MAR, ignoring how much returns exceeded it.

children.text: Running both formulas on a synthetic return series built to be upside-skewed, mostly small, steady gains, a handful of very large up days, and a few small losses, makes the difference concrete: Sharpe came out to 3.43, while Sortino came out to 19.12. Sharpe's denominator was inflated by the large up days that Sortino correctly ignored, since they never fell below the minimum acceptable return in the first place.
Calmar Ratio: Return Relative to Max Drawdown

body.caption: Calmar ratio measures return per unit of the single worst peak-to-trough decline experienced, rather than per unit of average volatility. For a strategy built around the drawdown-penalized reward from Chapter 3, Calmar is a natural, directly interpretable check on whether that reward term actually translated into controlled real-world drawdowns.

children.text: Tail Risk: VaR and CVaR, and Why VaR Alone Can Mislead

Value at Risk (VaR) at a 95% confidence level answers: what is the loss that will not be exceeded on 95% of trading days? Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), also called Expected Shortfall, answers a different and often more important question: given that the loss did exceed that threshold, how bad was it on average? A strategy can have a perfectly reasonable-looking VaR while hiding a genuinely dangerous tail, since VaR says nothing about what happens beyond its own threshold.

body.caption: VaR Can Look Similar While CVaR Reveals a Much Worse Tail
headers: Fat-Tailed Return Series (same mean, occasional sharp shocks)

body.text: Notice VaR alone barely distinguishes these two series, 1.69% versus 1.53%, and would have suggested the fat-tailed series is actually marginally safer. CVaR tells the true story: 4.06% versus 2.11%, nearly double. This is not a contrived result; it is exactly what VaR is structurally blind to, since it only reports a threshold, never how much worse things get once that threshold is crossed.

body.caption: Every function here operates on a plain array of periodic returns (or, for max_drawdown, an equity curve), the same output an evaluation rollout on Chapter 5's realistic backtest environment already produces. These five numbers, computed together, form the minimum report card for any trained agent.

body.text: No single metric here tells the whole story, the same warning Chapter 1 gave about a backtest concentrated in one favorable period applies just as much to a performance report concentrated in one favorable metric. A strategy with an excellent Sharpe ratio and a quietly terrible CVaR is not a strategy with mixed results, it is a strategy whose real risk the headline number was hiding. Report all of these together, every time, not whichever one happens to look best.

body.title: Choosing Between Two Strategies Using the Full Report Card
body.scenario: Two trained agents are evaluated on the same held-out test period using this lesson's metrics. Agent A: Sharpe 1.2, Sortino 1.6, Max Drawdown 12%, VaR 95% of 1.8%, CVaR 95% of 2.3%. Agent B: Sharpe 1.5, Sortino 1.7, Max Drawdown 11%, VaR 95% of 1.7%, CVaR 95% of 5.9%.
body.prompt: Which agent would you be more cautious about deploying, and why, given everything this lesson covered?
body.modelAnswer: Agent B looks better on Sharpe, Sortino, Max Drawdown, and VaR, all four of which would suggest picking Agent B without hesitation. But Agent B's CVaR of 5.9% versus Agent A's 2.3% reveals a large, hidden tail risk that none of the other four metrics captured, since VaR only reports a threshold and says nothing about severity beyond it. This is close to the calm-versus-fat-tailed comparison earlier in this lesson: a strategy can look equal or better on every metric except CVaR while carrying a meaningfully worse tail. The more cautious choice is Agent A, or at minimum, Agent B should not be deployed without first understanding what specific scenario is driving that 5.9% CVaR figure, since a headline-flattering report card with one badly lagging tail metric is exactly the pattern this lesson warned against trusting at face value.

body.title: What CVaR Adds That VaR Doesn't Have
body.question: A strategy's VaR (95%) and CVaR (95%) are calculated on the same return series. What does CVaR capture that VaR does not?
options: CVaR and VaR always report the same number for any return series, so nothing is added
CVaR measures average return, while VaR measures volatility
CVaR captures the severity of losses beyond the VaR threshold, by averaging the tail outcomes worse than that threshold, while VaR only reports the threshold itself
CVaR only applies to options strategies, not futures or equity strategies
body.explanation: VaR answers a threshold question: what loss will not be exceeded with a given confidence level. It says nothing about how much worse things get in the tail beyond that threshold. CVaR answers that follow-up question directly, by averaging the outcomes that did exceed the VaR threshold, which is exactly why two strategies with similar VaR can have very different, and very differently dangerous, CVaR figures.

points: Sharpe ratio penalizes upside and downside volatility symmetrically; Sortino ratio fixes this by dividing excess return only by downside deviation, which can make Sortino dramatically higher than Sharpe for an upside-skewed strategy
Calmar ratio measures annualized return relative to maximum drawdown, a direct, interpretable check on whether a drawdown-penalized reward actually produced controlled real-world drawdowns
VaR reports a loss threshold; CVaR reports the average severity of losses beyond that threshold, and the two can diverge sharply even when VaR alone looks similar across two strategies
A verified comparison in this lesson showed VaR barely distinguishing a calm return series from a fat-tailed one (1.69% vs 1.53%), while CVaR revealed the true gap clearly (2.11% vs 4.06%)

No single metric is sufficient on its own; a strong headline number alongside a quietly poor CVaR is a strategy whose real risk that headline number was hiding, not a strategy with genuinely mixed results

A minimum honest report card reports Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar, VaR, and CVaR together, every time, computed from the realistic backtest environment the previous lesson built, not the simplified training environment
